question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's media library in Cloud Storage contains millions of audio and video files. Access patterns vary widely: recently published episodes are streamed constantly, while older podcasts and documentaries are rarely retrieved but occasionally see unpredictable spikes when a topic becomes newsworthy. Altostrat wants to reduce storage cost without incurring surprise retrieval fees and without building custom tooling to track access patterns. What should you do?
options: Create an Object Lifecycle Management rule that moves every object older than 30 days to Coldline storage.
Keep all content in Standard storage and write a Cloud Run function that moves objects to Archive storage based on access logs analyzed in BigQuery.
Enable Autoclass on the bucket so objects transition automatically between storage classes based on their actual access patterns.
Create one bucket per storage class and have the content team move files manually when content is retired.
explanation: The deciding factor is unpredictable access combined with the case-study requirement to optimize storage cost while keeping content highly available. Autoclass automatically moves objects to colder classes when they are not accessed and moves them back to Standard on access, and Autoclass buckets do not charge early-deletion or retrieval fees, so newsworthy spikes on old content do not generate surprise bills. Option A is wrong because a fixed age-based rule ignores access patterns and Coldline retrieval and early-deletion fees would apply when old content spikes. Option B rebuilds what Autoclass already provides and adds operational overhead. Option D is manual, error-prone, and does not scale to millions of objects. This is a cost-optimization pillar decision that also preserves availability.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Storage Autoclass): The deciding factor is unpredictable access combined with the case-study requirement to optimize storage cost while keeping content highly available.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. After a documentary is published, its raw high-bitrate master files are kept only for legal and future remastering purposes. Masters are practically never accessed in the first several years but must be retained for at least 10 years, and the compliance team requires that nobody, including project owners, can delete or overwrite them during that period. The finished transcoded renditions must remain instantly available to the GKE delivery platform. You want to minimize cost. What should you do?
options: Store masters in a dedicated bucket whose default storage class is Archive, configure a 10-year bucket retention policy and lock it; keep renditions in a separate Standard storage bucket.
Enable Autoclass on a single bucket holding both masters and renditions, and rely on Autoclass to prevent early deletion of the master files.
Store masters in Coldline with a lifecycle rule that deletes them after 10 years, and store renditions in Nearline to reduce cost further.
Store masters in Standard storage with a locked retention policy and enable Object Versioning so overwrites keep the previous copy.
explanation: Archive is the lowest-cost class for data accessed less than once a year, and a locked bucket retention policy provides WORM-style immutability that even project owners cannot remove, satisfying the compliance requirement. Separating masters from renditions lets each set use the right class. Option B is wrong because Autoclass optimizes class transitions but provides no deletion protection. Option C has no immutability control, and Nearline renditions would incur retrieval fees and a 30-day minimum on frequently streamed content. Option D meets the immutability requirement but stores rarely accessed petabytes in the most expensive class, contradicting the cost-management priority in the executive statement.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Storage retention and lifecycle): Archive is the lowest-cost class for data accessed less than once a year, and a locked bucket retention policy provides WORM-style immutability that even project owners cannot remove, satisfying the compliance requirement.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's on-premises ingestion systems push about 40 TB of new raw footage per day into Cloud Storage and will continue to do so until the ingestion workflow is migrated. Transfers currently traverse the public internet with inconsistent throughput. Altostrat needs secure, high-performance hybrid connectivity backed by a 99.99% availability SLA, and traffic to Google APIs must not traverse the public internet. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Deploy one HA VPN gateway with two tunnels to a single Cloud Router and route all Google API traffic through the tunnels.
Provision a single 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connection in one edge availability domain and enable Private Google Access on the VPC subnets.
Use Partner Interconnect with a single 1 Gbps VLAN attachment and configure Cloud NAT so on-premises hosts can reach Cloud Storage.

Provision Dedicated Interconnect with four VLAN attachments across two metropolitan areas and both edge availability domains, connected to Cloud Routers in two regions, and advertise the private.googleapis.com range over BGP so ingestion traffic reaches Cloud Storage privately.
explanation: 40 TB per day is roughly 3.7 Gbps sustained, and the case study demands secure, high-performance connectivity with a 99.99% SLA. Only the 99.99% Dedicated Interconnect topology (four connections in two metros, two edge availability domains, Cloud Routers in two regions) meets that SLA, and advertising the private.googleapis.com range lets on-premises hosts reach Cloud Storage without the public internet. Option A cannot sustain this throughput reliably because HA VPN tunnels are capped around 3 Gbps each and still ride the internet. Option B provides only a 99.9% topology and a single point of failure. Option C is undersized at 1 Gbps, and Cloud NAT does not provide on-premises access to Google APIs. This is a reliability and performance-optimization decision.
hint: Core Rule (Dedicated Interconnect): 40 TB per day is roughly 3.7 Gbps sustained, and the case study demands secure, high-performance connectivity with a 99.99% SLA.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat wants to modernize CI/CD for its containerized GKE workloads using a centralized, managed platform. On every commit the pipeline must build container images from source, store them in a managed registry that scans for vulnerabilities, and promote releases through development, staging, and production GKE clusters with approval gates and one-click rollbacks. The team wants to run as little self-managed infrastructure as possible. Which three Google Cloud services should you use? (Choose three.)
options: Cloud Build
Jenkins on a Compute Engine managed instance group
Artifact Registry

explanation: Cloud Build provides serverless, trigger-based image builds; Artifact Registry is the recommended managed registry with built-in vulnerability scanning through Artifact Analysis; and Cloud Deploy provides managed delivery pipelines that promote releases across GKE targets with approvals and rollbacks. Together they meet the case study's 'centralized management platform' requirement without self-managed servers. Jenkins on Compute Engine is self-managed infrastructure. Container Registry is deprecated in favor of Artifact Registry. Cloud Deployment Manager is a deprecated infrastructure-provisioning tool, not a release-promotion tool. This aligns with the operational-excellence pillar's automation guidance.
hint: Core Rule (CI/CD tooling): Cloud Build provides serverless, trigger-based image builds; Artifact Registry is the recommended managed registry with built-in vulnerability scanning through Artifact Analysis; and Cloud Deploy provides managed delivery pipelines that promote releases across GKE targets with approvals and rollbacks.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat authenticates users through Google Identity and several third-party identity providers. Content editors at a recently acquired studio sign in through the studio's own Okta tenant. Altostrat wants these editors to use the Google Cloud console and access Cloud Storage buckets with their existing corporate credentials. Security policy prohibits creating duplicate user accounts in Cloud Identity, and access must be revoked automatically when the studio deactivates an employee. What should you do?
options: Provision a Cloud Identity account for each editor with Google Cloud Directory Sync and enable SAML single sign-on to Okta.
Create a Workforce Identity Federation pool with the studio's Okta tenant as the provider and grant IAM roles to principal sets from that pool.
Create a service account per editor, distribute JSON keys, and rotate the keys every 90 days.
Configure Workload Identity Federation with Okta as an OIDC provider and have editors impersonate a shared service account.
explanation: Workforce Identity Federation lets human users from an external IdP access Google Cloud (console and APIs) without provisioning accounts in Cloud Identity; when Okta disables the user, they can no longer obtain federated credentials, so revocation is automatic. Option A synchronizes duplicate accounts, which the policy prohibits. Option C uses long-lived service-account keys, an anti-pattern that provides no per-user auditability or automatic revocation. Option D is wrong because Workload Identity Federation is designed for non-human workloads, not for interactive console access by employees. This is a security pillar decision favoring federated, keyless identity.
hint: Core Rule: Workforce Identity Federation lets human users from an external IdP access Google Cloud (console and APIs) without provisioning accounts in Cloud Identity; when Okta disables the user, they can no longer obtain federated credentials, so revocation is automatic.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's SRE team runs self-managed Prometheus servers inside each GKE cluster. Retention is limited to 15 days, the servers run out of memory during traffic spikes, and metrics from different clusters cannot be queried together. question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat currently delivers all alerts by email. During a weekend outage of the recommendation service, the alert email went unread for four hours and the availability objective was breached. Altostrat wants critical alerts to reach the on-call engineer immediately with escalation if unacknowledged, while low-severity alerts continue to go to the team mailbox. It does not want to build a custom notification service. What should you do?

explanation: Cloud Monitoring supports multiple notification channel types and severity labels on alerting policies, so critical alerts can page an on-call engineer through an integrated incident-management tool with escalation, while informational alerts remain on email. This directly addresses the case study's weakness of email-only alerting and improves reliability. Option A is the custom notification service the team wants to avoid and still ends in email. question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's new viewer chatbot accepts free-text questions and comments, and its responses are generated by Gemini on Vertex AI. question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's content strategy analysts are proficient in SQL but not Python. question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's video transcoding runs in Cloud Run functions triggered by uploads. Feature-length documentaries exceed the function timeout, causing failed and duplicated jobs, and the team maintains custom FFmpeg containers and encoding presets. Reliability and cost are Altostrat's top priorities, and the team wants to minimize custom code. What should you do?
options: Replace the custom transcoding logic with the Transcoder API: the upload-triggered Cloud Run function submits a transcoding job with the required output profiles, and results are written back to Cloud Storage.
Raise the Cloud Run function timeout and memory to the maximum and add retries with exponential backoff.
Move transcoding to a GKE Standard GPU node pool with a custom job queue built on Memorystore.
Run FFmpeg on a large Compute Engine instance with a cron job that scans the bucket every hour.
explanation: The Transcoder API is a fully managed service purpose-built for converting media files into streaming formats; it handles long inputs asynchronously, removes the custom FFmpeg containers, and bills per minute of output, which satisfies reliability, cost, and minimal-code constraints at the same time. Option B still leaves long files at risk of hitting limits and keeps the custom encoder. Option C solves the timeout but adds a GPU cluster and a hand-built queue to operate. Option D is a single point of failure, introduces up to an hour of latency, and wastes an always-on VM. This is a build-versus-buy disposition decision favoring the managed service.
hint: Core Rule: The Transcoder API is a fully managed service purpose-built for converting media files into streaming formats; it handles long inputs asynchronously, removes the custom FFmpeg containers, and bills per minute of output, which satisfies reliability, cost, and minimal-code constraints at the same time.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's on-premises archival system holds 3 PB of historical broadcast footage that must be migrated to a Cloud Storage bucket within six weeks, when the data-center lease expires. The site has one 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect that also carries the daily production ingestion traffic of roughly 4 Gbps on average. Data must be encrypted in transit and at rest. What should you do?
options: Use Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data over the Interconnect and cap its bandwidth at 6 Gbps so production ingestion is not affected.
Run gsutil -m rsync in parallel from several on-premises servers over the Interconnect until the copy finishes.

Order multiple Transfer Appliances, load the archive locally, ship them to Google for ingestion into the bucket, and use the Interconnect only for the small delta produced while the appliances are in transit.
Compress the footage with an on-premises Dataflow pipeline and upload it over the public internet with Storage Transfer Service.
explanation: At the roughly 6 Gbps left over after production traffic, 3 PB would take about 46 days at perfect utilization, exceeding the six-week deadline with no margin. Transfer Appliance is the recommended option when data exceeds what the network can move in time; the appliances are encrypted, so the in-transit and at-rest requirements are met, and the Interconnect remains free for production ingestion and the final delta. Option A is the right tool for online transfer but the math shows it cannot make the deadline. Option B is slower and less robust than Storage Transfer Service and has the same bandwidth problem. Option D compresses already-compressed video for little gain, uses the slower public internet, and Dataflow does not run on-premises.
hint: Core Rule (Data transfer planning): At the roughly 6 Gbps left over after production traffic, 3 PB would take about 46 days at perfect utilization, exceeding the six-week deadline with no margin.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's GKE bill has doubled in a year. Analysis shows a steady baseline of user-facing content-delivery services plus a large, spiky batch workload that generates thumbnails and previews and can tolerate interruption and retries. The reliability of the user-facing services must not decrease. Which two actions should you take to reduce cost? (Choose two.)
options: Move all node pools, including the content-delivery services, to Spot VMs.
Run the thumbnail batch workload on a Spot VM node pool (or Autopilot Spot Pods) with tolerations, checkpointing, and automatic retries.
Disable the cluster autoscaler and fix node counts at peak capacity to avoid scaling delays.
Move the user-facing services into a single zone to eliminate inter-zone traffic charges.
Purchase committed use discounts that cover the predictable baseline compute of the content-delivery services.
Increase every pod's CPU request to guarantee extra headroom.
explanation: The cost-optimization pillar recommends matching purchasing models to workload characteristics: fault-tolerant, interruptible batch jobs belong on Spot capacity (60–91% cheaper), and steady, predictable baseline usage should be covered by committed use discounts. Option A would expose latency-sensitive user-facing services to preemption, reducing reliability. Option C removes elasticity and pays for peak capacity all the time. Option D lowers availability, contradicting the reliability priority in the executive statement. Option F increases requested resources and therefore cost, the opposite of right-sizing.
hint: Core Rule (GKE cost optimization): The cost-optimization pillar recommends matching purchasing models to workload characteristics: fault-tolerant, interruptible batch jobs belong on Spot capacity (60–91% cheaper), and steady, predictable baseline usage should be covered by committed use discounts.

question: For this question, refer to the Altostrat Media case study. Altostrat's on-premises ingestion servers upload footage to Cloud Storage over the Dedicated Interconnect. The security team requires that these uploads never traverse the public internet, and the servers have no public IP addresses and no NAT path to the internet. The Google Cloud VPC uses a private-only design. How should you configure access to the Cloud Storage API?
options: Enable Private Google Access on the VPC subnets; on-premises hosts automatically inherit it through the VLAN attachment.

Configure on-premises DNS to resolve *.googleapis.com to the private.googleapis.com virtual IP range, advertise that range as a custom route from Cloud Router over the Interconnect, and add on-premises routes for it toward the VLAN attachments.
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway in the VPC and route on-premises traffic through it to reach storage.googleapis.com.
Create a proxy VM with an external IP address in the VPC and configure the ingestion servers to use it as an HTTP forward proxy.
explanation: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts requires three things: DNS records that map Google API names to the private.googleapis.com (or restricted.googleapis.com) VIP, a custom route advertisement of that range from Cloud Router over the Interconnect, and matching routes on-premises. Traffic then reaches Cloud Storage entirely over the Interconnect. Option A is wrong because subnet-level Private Google Access applies only to VM instances in the VPC, not to on-premises hosts. Option C is wrong because Cloud NAT only serves VMs in the VPC and would send traffic to the public internet anyway. Option D introduces a public IP and a single-VM bottleneck, violating the security requirement. A Private Service Connect endpoint for Google APIs would be an equally valid alternative design.
hint: Core Rule: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts requires three things: DNS records that map Google API names to the private.googleapis.com (or restricted.googleapis.com) VIP, a custom route advertisement of that range from Cloud Router over the Interconnect, and matching routes on-premises.
